query: Prior calculations on concentrated alloys examined variations in atomic mass and force constants, temperature-dependent lattice heat transport, or DFT-derived elastic properties coupled to analytical conductivity estimates; some estimates require a Debye temperature. The cited simulations generally represented perfect, defect-free bulk crystals. Experiments below 200 K indicate that lattice and electronic contributions in HfNbTaTiZr can be comparable, while measurements from 300 to 1200 K on a specimen containing 1 wt.% oxygen report total conductivity of 10–17 W/(K m). Available analytical approaches do not capture all relevant atomic-scale complexity in refractory high-entropy alloys, and separate transport studies do not establish a predictive solution for this alloy. Given these constraints, what testable hypothesis could an unspecified new predictive approach make for HfNbTaTiZr without conflating lattice and electronic heat transport? Explain why it should outperform earlier approaches, quantify the expected improvement, define its temperature and sample applicability limits, identify supporting observations from the cited work, and specify decisive comparisons with low- and high-temperature measurements that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: A hybrid ab initio framework that separately computes electron–phonon scattering and anharmonic phonon dynamics—including explicit treatment of oxygen defects—will predict, without conflating contributions, the lattice and electronic thermal conductivities of HfNbTaTiZr with an overall accuracy improvement of roughly 30–50% over previous Debye-based and DFT-elasticity methods.
generation.material_initial_state: HfNbTaTiZr in both its ideal, defect‐free form and in oxygen-contaminated specimens (~1 wt.% O).
generation.intervention: Implement a hybrid computational method that couples advanced first‐principles electron–phonon scattering calculations for the electronic channel with machine‐learning–accelerated anharmonic lattice dynamics for the phonon channel, explicitly incorporating oxygen defect effects into the interatomic potentials.
generation.conditions: Temperature regimes below 200 K (where lattice and electronic contributions are comparable) and from 300 to 1200 K (the range of experimental total conductivity measurements).
generation.structural_mediator: Incorporation of oxygen defect effects within the interatomic potential parameterization, allowing the model to adjust scattering rates and phonon lifetimes in both ideal and contaminated samples.
generation.mechanism: By separately calculating the scattering rates and contributions for electrons and phonons under realistic defect conditions, the model can avoid conflation of thermal transport channels. This more detailed accounting enables accurate predictions of both lattice and electronic thermal conductivities as functions of temperature and defect level.
generation.predicted_outcome: At 300 K, the framework is expected to predict separate lattice thermal conductivities around 6–10 W/(K·m) and electronic contributions around 4–7 W/(K·m), such that the summed value is consistent with experimental total thermal conductivities (10–17 W/(K·m)) for oxygen-doped samples. Similar separate predictions at low temperatures (<200 K) should reconcile measured comparable contributions from both channels.
generation.baseline: Earlier approaches based on simplified Debye temperature estimates and DFT-derived elastic constants that conflated the lattice and electronic contributions, with prediction accuracies substantially lower (by an estimated 30–50%) compared to the new method.
generation.boundary: The model’s applicability is limited to the temperature ranges where the underlying phonon and electron scattering mechanisms are well captured (below 200 K and between 300–1200 K) and for alloy compositions with up to approximately 1 wt.% oxygen contamination.
generation.uncertainty: The exact numerical improvement and sensitivity to defect-related scattering parameters remain uncertain due to inherent approximations in both ab initio and ML-accelerated methods; experimental verification across the full temperature range is essential.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare HfNbTaTiZr samples in both high-purity (defect-free) and controlled oxygen-doped (~1 wt.% O) forms. Measure the total thermal conductivity as a function of temperature in two regimes: below 200 K and between 300–1200 K. Employ techniques capable of independently probing phonon and electron contributions (e.g., combined pulsed laser techniques with advanced spectroscopy) to obtain separate estimates of lattice and electronic conductivities.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the separated lattice and electronic conductivities predicted by the model differ from the experimentally measured values by more than ±20%, or if the overall accuracy improvement over previous models is below approximately 30%, then the hybrid model’s validity is falsified.

In this work first-principles calculations are used to study the stability and physical properties of the three polymorphs, αNb5Si3, βNb5Si3 and γNb5Si3 alloyed with Ti (up to 12.5 at. % Ti for αNb5Si3 and βNb5Si3 and up to 50 at. % Ti for γNb5Si3). Density functional theory (DFT) is used to study the enthalpy of formation and properties of the αNb5Si3, βNb5Si3 and γNb5Si3 compounds with and without Ti additions at T = 0 K. To probe the effect of Ti on the transformation temperatures, the temperature dependence of the heats of formation of the compounds is computed by incorporating phonon calculations. The paper provides new data that advance current understanding of the stability of complex Nb-silicide based alloys and the design and development of new alloys.

Recently, PbSnTeSe has been experimentally investigated by Fan et al. [] and Raphel et al. [,], who report appreciably similar results for the thermoelectric performance of the material (see below). The modelling of HEAs transport properties constitute a challenge, and both the simulation methods and their derived predictions have to be confronted to experimental data to assess their validity. In this context, we present in this paper for the first time a complete approach that allows one to obtain all the transport coefficients, including the figure of merit, of a high-entropy alloy. The thermoelectric transport properties of the PbSnTeSe high-entropy alloy have been calculated by combining state-of-the-art methods based on the special quasi-random structures approach to generate the HEA structure, the first-principles density-functional theory (DFT), and the Boltzmann transport and Green–Kubo theories. First, from the DFT-computed material electronic states, the electronic transport properties (electronic conductivity, Seebeck coefficient and electronic thermal conductivity) were calculated using the linearized Boltzmann transport equation, and the power factor was obtained. decision.trend: Early work on thermal transport in HEAs has evolved from using simplified, Debye‐temperature–based analytical models and DFT-derived elastic properties to estimate conductivity, toward atomistic simulations (e.g. MD) that capture lattice distortions and temperature effects. In parallel, separate studies on electrical conduction in refractory HEAs, such as in Nb-Mo-Ta-W systems, revealed the challenge of the cocktail effect, yet none of these works addressed both channels independently, especially under realistic conditions (e.g. oxygen contamination). The approaches have generally assumed defect-free crystals or treated lattice and electronic conduction together, leaving the separation of these contributions—and their temperature dependence—an open problem.
decision.unsolved: There remains an inability to quantitatively and separately predict the lattice and electronic thermal conductivities for HfNbTaTiZr, especially when comparing ideal (defect-free) simulations with experimental specimens that include ~1 wt.% oxygen. In addition, none of the earlier models explicitly define performance across low-temperature (<200 K) and high-temperature (300–1200 K) regimes with clear error margins, and decisive tests that can falsify the predictions are lacking.
decision.lever: Develop a hybrid ab initio framework that couples advanced first‐principles electron–phonon scattering calculations (for the electronic channel) with machine‐learning–accelerated anharmonic lattice dynamics (for the phonon channel), explicitly incorporating defect effects (e.g. oxygen) into the interatomic potentials.
decision.why: This approach directly builds on the trend toward atomistic, high-fidelity models while addressing the limitation of conflated transport channels. By separately calculating electron and phonon scattering rates for both ideal and contaminated samples, it is expected to improve predictive accuracy by roughly 30–50% over earlier Debye-based and DFT-elasticity methods. Its design includes explicit temperature limits (<200 K and 300–1200 K) and provides clear, falsifiable predictions: for example, if the separated contributions (e.g. a predicted lattice conductivity of ~6–10 W/(K·m) and electronic mode of ~4–7 W/(K·m) at 300 K) diverge significantly from low-temperature measurements or high-temperature total conductivities in oxygen-doped samples, the hypothesis would be falsified.
